recipes.title: Test browser flows and reproduce interface failures
recipes.description: Choose the browser control and debugging model that matches the task. Supported engines do not make desktop emulation equivalent to a physical mobile device.

picks.label: Cross-engine application tests
picks.reason: Isolated contexts, auto-waiting assertions and trace inspection support repeatable flows across Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
picks.tradeoff: Browser binaries and system dependencies must be installed; physical device testing remains separate.

picks.label: Interactive test development
picks.reason: The visible runner shows the application alongside test command history during component and end-to-end test development.
picks.tradeoff: Its execution model differs from WebDriver, and hosted Cloud features have separate plans.

picks.label: Scripted browser tasks
picks.reason: A direct browser API suits page rendering, PDF generation, screenshots and custom automation helpers.
picks.tradeoff: It is a programming library; assertions, test organization and reporting need additional choices.

picks.label: Readable acceptance workflows
picks.reason: Reusable keywords can connect browser actions to broader application acceptance steps.
picks.tradeoff: Automation capabilities come from libraries, each with its own prerequisites and support scope.

recipes.title: Design realistic service load tests
recipes.description: Workload design and load-generator capacity determine whether results answer the intended question. These selections reflect scripting and protocol needs, not a benchmark ranking.

picks.label: JavaScript workload scenarios
picks.reason: Scenarios, thresholds and metric exports suit versioned performance checks in development pipelines.
picks.tradeoff: Local execution needs sufficient resources; optional Grafana Cloud services are priced separately.

picks.label: Python user behavior
picks.reason: Python tasks and distributed workers suit custom user journeys and reuse of existing Python helpers.
picks.tradeoff: The test code and generator capacity need profiling so they do not become the bottleneck.

picks.label: Protocol-rich test plans
picks.reason: A GUI plan editor and a broad sampler ecosystem help assemble tests involving multiple service protocols.
picks.tradeoff: Generate substantial load in command-line mode and budget the Java runtime and plugin overhead.

picks.label: Controlled HTTP request rates
picks.reason: A CLI/library model supports repeatable HTTP workloads at a specified request rate with exported results.
picks.tradeoff: Complex multi-step user behavior requires additional scripting or another workload model.

picks.label: Quick terminal HTTP checks
picks.reason: A standalone command-line interface with live terminal feedback suits focused endpoint experiments.
picks.tradeoff: A short endpoint test is not a complete simulation of a production service workload.

recipes.title: Develop against predictable API responses
recipes.description: A mock server supplies controlled behavior; a request checker verifies it. Combine these roles when a remote dependency is unavailable or difficult to reproduce.

picks.label: Design mocks visually
picks.reason: The desktop editor provides routes, templating and response rules for local mock API servers.
picks.tradeoff: Centralized collaboration and managed deployments belong to separately licensed Pro offerings.

picks.label: Programmatic stubs and scenarios
picks.reason: Request matching, stateful scenarios and a standalone Java server suit repository-managed service test fixtures.
picks.tradeoff: A compatible Java runtime and deliberate stub design are required.

picks.label: Assert request and response behavior
picks.reason: Text files can chain HTTP requests, extract values and check responses in CI.
picks.tradeoff: Hurl sends and checks requests; it does not replace the server providing mocked responses.

picks.label: Maintain interactive API collections
picks.reason: Local collection files support manual API exploration and review in version control.
picks.tradeoff: Advanced or team capabilities can require a paid edition.

recipes.title: Find Python CPU and memory bottlenecks
recipes.description: Choose the measurement question first: sampling a running process, attributing CPU/memory work to lines, or explaining allocation stacks.

picks.label: Sample a running Python process
picks.reason: An external sampling profiler can inspect Python execution and generate flame graphs without rewriting application code.
picks.tradeoff: Process inspection may need additional privileges; samples do not enumerate every allocation.

picks.label: Separate Python and native work
picks.reason: Line-oriented CPU and memory reporting helps locate Python code, native code and allocation activity in one report.
picks.tradeoff: GPU reporting depends on supported hardware; optional AI suggestions need separate correctness review.

picks.label: Explain allocation growth
picks.reason: Native and Python allocation stacks, reports and flame graphs help investigate memory use and leaks.
picks.tradeoff: The supported host set is Linux and macOS; wheels and native dependencies must match the environment.

recipes.title: Inspect native and JVM performance profiles
recipes.description: Sampling, allocation instrumentation and JVM inspection answer different questions. Capture representative workloads with symbols and permissions appropriate to the selected tool.

picks.label: Capture across desktop systems
picks.reason: Sampling on Windows, macOS and Linux can feed an interactive Firefox Profiler interface.
picks.tradeoff: Event support and collection permissions differ by operating system.

picks.label: Explore Linux perf recordings
picks.reason: Call trees, source/assembly views and flame graphs help interpret Linux perf data in a GUI.
picks.tradeoff: The capture and debug symbols must be usable; the collection workflow is Linux-focused.

picks.label: Trace JVM and native stacks
picks.reason: Profiling JVM workloads with native stack visibility suits CPU, allocation and lock investigations.
picks.tradeoff: Linux and macOS support depends on JVM, event and operating-system configuration.

picks.label: Inspect a running Java application
picks.reason: A desktop interface brings JVM monitoring, thread/heap inspection and profiling tools together.
picks.tradeoff: Connection configuration and JDK compatibility matter; deep profiling can change workload behavior.

picks.label: Investigate native memory correctness
picks.reason: Instrumentation tools such as Memcheck and Massif help explain memory errors and heap usage.
picks.tradeoff: Execution can slow substantially, supported OS/CPU combinations are limited, and upstream provides source releases.

recipes.title: Make project runtimes and environments reproducible
recipes.description: A runtime-version manager and a dependency/environment manager control different parts of a workstation. Pick by language and native-library needs.

picks.label: Python packages and environments
picks.reason: Python version management, project lockfiles and isolated tool execution provide a cohesive Python workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Native package dependencies and indexes still need compatible builds and deliberate trust choices.

picks.label: Python plus native libraries
picks.reason: Conda and PyPI dependencies, lockfiles and project tasks suit scientific or mixed native/Python environments.
picks.tradeoff: Available packages and solver results depend on the selected channels and target platforms.

picks.label: Several language tool versions
picks.reason: Per-project runtime versions, environment configuration and tasks suit polyglot development.
picks.tradeoff: Backend and plugin support differs across tools and operating systems.

picks.label: Focused Node.js switching
picks.reason: A dedicated Node.js version manager supports automatic project version selection.
picks.tradeoff: Shell initialization is required; JavaScript package dependencies are a separate concern.

picks.label: Native Windows Python selection
picks.reason: A Windows-specific implementation supplies the Python version-switching workflow that Unix pyenv does not provide natively.
picks.tradeoff: Available versions and shell/path configuration differ from the original pyenv project.

recipes.title: Improve native build and test feedback
recipes.description: Configure the build graph first, then decide whether execution, caching or test scheduling is the limiting factor. Cache tools do not guarantee a speedup for every project.

picks.label: Generate project build systems
picks.reason: Platform and toolchain abstractions connect a source project to IDEs and build backends.
picks.tradeoff: Complex cross-compilation and dependency discovery still require project-specific configuration.

picks.label: Describe builds declaratively
picks.reason: A focused build-definition language and dependency discovery suit new native projects with a supported toolchain.
picks.tradeoff: Migrating an existing build can be substantial, and backend behavior must match project needs.

picks.label: Execute a generated build graph
picks.reason: A small build executor runs commands from a dependency graph generated by another tool.
picks.tradeoff: It does not replace a higher-level project configurator such as CMake or Meson.

picks.label: Reuse C/C++ compilation results
picks.reason: Repeated compatible compiler invocations can use local or configured remote cached results.
picks.tradeoff: Changing relevant inputs or using unsupported compilation modes causes misses or bypasses.

picks.label: Share Rust and C/C++ compilation caches
picks.reason: Multiple storage backends and optional distributed compilation suit teams with compatible repeated builds.
picks.tradeoff: Remote storage, credentials and cache compatibility add setup and maintenance work.

picks.label: Schedule Rust test binaries
picks.reason: Isolated test processes, filtering and profiles provide control over large Rust test suites.
picks.tradeoff: Doctests require the standard Cargo workflow; concurrency and isolation can expose test assumptions.

recipes.title: Explore local data and share queryable results
recipes.description: Choose a query engine, terminal interface or publishing layer according to where the data lives and who needs to use it.

picks.label: Query analytical files in process
picks.reason: SQL over formats such as CSV and Parquet supports local analytical work without deploying a separate database server.
picks.tradeoff: It is not a drop-in substitute for a multi-user transactional service.

picks.label: Work in a terminal SQL interface
picks.reason: An editor, query results and database adapters make interactive SQL practical in a terminal.
picks.tradeoff: Capabilities depend on the adapter, driver and terminal environment.

picks.label: Convert and reshape SQLite data
picks.reason: A CLI and Python library support imports, schema changes and SQL over local SQLite databases.
picks.tradeoff: It is script-oriented and SQLite-focused rather than a full visual administration suite.

picks.label: Browse and publish SQLite content
picks.reason: A local web interface and JSON endpoints expose queryable data to other users and tools.
picks.tradeoff: Deployment, permissions and exposed data require deliberate configuration.

picks.label: Inspect many tabular formats
picks.reason: Keyboard-driven sheets support sorting, filtering and exploration before or alongside SQL work.
picks.tradeoff: Large data still consumes memory; its Windows route uses WSL rather than a native build.

recipes.title: Evaluate and script language-model workflows
recipes.description: Select an evaluator, command-line client or serving runtime by role. Local tools can still incur provider charges and send data externally when configured to use remote services.

picks.label: Compare prompts on a test suite
picks.reason: Versioned cases, assertions and provider comparisons help detect changes in a defined model workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Test design and graders determine what is measured; passing a suite does not establish broad safety or correctness.

picks.label: Keep model calls scriptable
picks.reason: A CLI, plugin ecosystem and response logging suit repeatable model calls in shell workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Providers, plugins and models have separate setup, licensing and cost considerations.

picks.label: Use several providers from a terminal
picks.reason: Chat, retrieval and tool-oriented terminal workflows can share one configured client.
picks.tradeoff: Provider credentials, external data transfer and tool execution need deliberate configuration.

picks.label: Serve supported models on Linux
picks.reason: Continuous batching and a server API suit controlled local or on-premises model serving.
picks.tradeoff: GPU/CPU support, memory needs and deployment tuning are substantial; Windows support is through WSL.

picks.label: Start with a desktop local-model interface
picks.reason: Model discovery, chat and a local server provide a graphical path to supported local models.
picks.tradeoff: The app is proprietary, model licenses vary, and current macOS builds require Apple Silicon.

recipes.title: Choose a tool for a small original game
recipes.description: Match the authoring model and target first: a broad engine, event-based visual logic, a Lua framework, retro constraints or a narrative-first workflow.

picks.label: Integrated 2D and 3D authoring
picks.reason: A scene editor, scripting and export workflow support a range of original game projects.
picks.tradeoff: Target exports and advanced rendering features have platform-specific requirements.

picks.label: Event-based visual logic
picks.reason: A visual event system and editor help create games without starting from a code-only framework.
picks.tradeoff: Hosted build, publishing and collaboration allowances differ between free and paid plans.

picks.label: Lua and component-based projects
picks.reason: An integrated editor and Lua scripting support focused cross-platform 2D/3D production.
picks.tradeoff: The custom source-available license restricts commercialization of the engine/editor itself.

picks.label: Code-oriented 2D games
picks.reason: A Lua framework supplies graphics, audio and input while leaving game structure to the programmer.
picks.tradeoff: There is no integrated scene editor, and packaging remains part of the development work.

picks.label: Game Boy-style constraints
picks.reason: Visual scripting and retro asset workflows produce games for the supported Game Boy and web targets.
picks.tradeoff: Hardware-style limits, asset rules and engine constraints shape the design.

picks.label: Visual novels and dialogue
picks.reason: A narrative-focused engine combines dialogue scripts, branching, saves and presentation features.
picks.tradeoff: General action or 3D games usually need a more suitable engine or extensive custom work.

recipes.title: Choose a modding tool by game asset format
recipes.description: Identify the engine and asset type before choosing a tool. Format support, game-specific encryption and export limitations matter more than an overall popularity ranking.

picks.label: Inspect supported Unreal assets
picks.reason: Package browsing and previews help inspect supported Unreal Engine game content.
picks.tradeoff: The Windows tool requires compatible mappings or keys for some games and cannot make every custom format readable.

picks.label: Recover supported Unity content
picks.reason: Asset extraction and project reconstruction workflows help inspect supported Unity data.
picks.tradeoff: Recovered projects may need repairs; some analysis/export capabilities require Premium.

picks.label: Modify Unity asset bundles
picks.reason: Type and bundle editing suits deliberate changes to supported Unity asset data.
picks.tradeoff: It is primarily a modding editor, and dependencies and newer game formats can impose limits.

picks.label: Inspect Bethesda NIF structures
picks.reason: The explicitly identified fo76utils fork adds newer-format rendering, materials and selected glTF workflows.
picks.tradeoff: It is experimental; format and import limitations differ by game, and the binary CPU requirements matter.

picks.label: Adjust supported body and outfit meshes
picks.reason: BodySlide and Outfit Studio provide slider, mesh-fitting and outfit-editing workflows for supported game setups.
picks.tradeoff: Correct game files, presets and skeleton/physics expectations are required; it is not a general-purpose 3D editor.

picks.label: Prepare DirectX textures
picks.reason: DDS conversion, mipmaps and block-compression options support game texture preparation.
picks.tradeoff: Color space, alpha behavior and compression must match the target; Windows imaging support differs from WSL builds.

recipes.title: Choose a browser for workspaces or keyboard control
recipes.description: Workspace organization, Firefox-derived customization and programmable keyboard navigation offer different ways to manage browsing. Compatibility and timely engine updates still need attention.

picks.label: Organize split views and workspaces
picks.reason: Vertical tabs, workspace organization and split views suit users keeping several related pages visible.
picks.tradeoff: Widevine DRM is unavailable on the documented Windows/macOS path, and workspaces alone do not isolate all browser data.

picks.label: Customize a Firefox-derived workspace
picks.reason: Sidebar and layout controls provide several ways to arrange pages and browser functions.
picks.tradeoff: Customization adds settings to learn, and website compatibility still depends on the underlying browser stack.

picks.label: Use Firefox-derived desktop features
picks.reason: Private tabs and customization features provide a free desktop browsing alternative.
picks.tradeoff: Its smaller project and separate release process require checking current compatibility and security updates.

picks.label: Navigate primarily with a keyboard
picks.reason: Vim-style controls and Python configuration suit a minimal keyboard-oriented interface.
picks.tradeoff: QtWebEngine packaging influences codecs and updates; normal Firefox/Chrome extension support is not provided.

picks.label: Program the browsing workflow
picks.reason: Lisp configuration and keyboard-oriented commands suit users who want extensive programmable browser behavior.
picks.tradeoff: GNU/Linux is the primary supported path; macOS and Windows are in development, and the interface requires learning.
